notes.meaning: Moses tells the two tribes that once the land is won, they may go home with a clear conscience. They will have kept faith with God and with their fellow Israelites. "Before the LORD" means with God's presence and help, and with his approval. The land east of the Jordan will then truly be theirs, as God's gift.

If they break their promise, they will be sinning against God himself, not just against their brothers. "Your sin will find you out" means the punishment for sin will surely catch up with them. Sin and its payback are tied together, even when God seems to wait a while. Matthew Henry and Wesley add that we should find our own sins out first, so we can turn from them, before they find us out.
Moses lets them go ahead with their plan. They may build towns for their families and pens for their sheep. But he ends with a firm reminder: do what you said you would do.
The two tribes, speaking through one spokesman, agree to Moses' terms. It is like signing a solemn pledge. The other tribes had helped them win this land, so it was only fair to help in return.
Their families and herds will stay behind in the towns of Gilead. That way the fighting men are free to serve their brothers without anything slowing them down.

The soldiers promise to cross the river and fight "before the LORD." Israel's army was God's army, and the ark, the sign of God's presence, went with them into battle. Matthew Henry notes that about 40,000 men went, out of about 100,000. Some had to stay to farm and guard the land.

Moses knew he would die before the land was won. So he gave the deal to Eleazar the priest, to Joshua, and to the tribal leaders. They would make sure the promise was kept after he was gone, by both sides.

Moses states the deal plainly to the leaders. If the two tribes fight beside them until the land is won, Gilead is theirs to keep. Calvin says Moses speaks as if victory were already sure, to give everyone courage to cross over.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars have argued that this chapter was put together from different written sources. They point to changes in wording, like "before Israel" and "before the LORD."

notes.meaning: If they refuse to fight, they lose the land east of the Jordan. They would be made to cross with their families and take land in Canaan with everyone else. Their laziness or fear would win them nothing, and the nation would not split apart.

The tribes say they will do what "the LORD" has said. Moses was God's messenger, so his words were treated as God's words. It may also point back to God's earlier command for all Israel to take Canaan.
They repeat their promise once more. Now they use Moses' own words, "before the LORD." In return, they ask that their land on the east side be theirs to keep.

Moses grants them the lands of the two defeated kings, Sihon and Og. Half the tribe of Manasseh is named here for the first time. Some of their clans had already conquered parts of this area, so they were given what they had won. The exact borders were left for the leaders to set later.

"Built" here means they repaired and strengthened towns that already stood. Walls had likely been damaged in the war or left to decay. Strong walls kept the women and children safe while the men were away. They also made pens for their flocks.

The tribe of Reuben rebuilt towns near Heshbon, the old capital of King Sihon. They gave some towns new names. Nebo and Baal were names of false gods. God had told Israel not even to speak the names of other gods, so the new names helped wipe them from memory. New names also showed the towns had new owners.

The family of Machir, part of Manasseh's tribe, were brave fighters. They took Gilead and drove out the Amorites who lived there. This explains why half of Manasseh's tribe shared in the land east of the Jordan.

Moses gave Gilead to Machir's family line, not to Machir himself, who had long since died. They settled there and brought their families. Placing such bold fighters on the border helped keep everyone safe.
Jair, a descendant of Manasseh through his mother's side, captured a group of villages. He named them Havvoth-jair, meaning "the villages of Jair."

Nobah, likely a leading man of Manasseh's tribe, took the town of Kenath and the small towns around it. He renamed it after himself. The commentators add a sad note. These tribes were the first to settle in their land, and later they were the first carried away captive by Assyria, because they turned to other gods.
